meta.title: Responsibility accounting and sales variances
meta.summary: Responsibility centers, controllability and performance reports, the sales-volume variance, its split into sales-mix and sales-quantity variances, and market-share and market-size variances.

videos.title: Responsibility centers
videos.take: Cost, revenue, profit and investment centers hold managers accountable for what they control

scenes.say: A budget only works if someone is responsible for each part of it. That's responsibility accounting.

scenes.heading: Four kinds of responsibility center
scenes.say: A cost center manager is accountable for costs, like the assembly plant. A revenue center for revenues, like the dealer sales team. A profit center for both, like the parts and accessories business. An investment center for profit and the assets used to earn it.

sub: Judge managers on what they can decide
scenes.say: The key is matching measures to authority. The assembly manager decides how bikes are built, not their price, so she's judged on cost, not profit.

sub: A cost center may cut quality;
scenes.say: Each type also creates temptations. A cost center manager might cut quality to save money. A revenue center might discount heavily to hit sales targets. Good systems add measures to balance them.
Measuring investment centers, with return on investment and residual income, comes in Lecture 14.

scenes.q: The manager of Tallgrass's online store sets prices, buys stock and controls costs, but not the warehouse investment. What type of center?
scenes.say: Quick check. The online store manager sets prices, buys stock and controls costs, but not the warehouse investment. What type of center is that? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Controllability and performance reports
videos.take: Performance reports should separate controllable items and be used to learn, not to blame

scenes.say: Should a manager be blamed for a cost she can't control? Usually not. But it's not that simple.

sub: The degree of influence a manager
has over a cost, revenue or item
scenes.say: Controllability is the degree of influence a manager has over an item. Few costs are fully controllable by one person. Battery prices, for example, depend on suppliers and world markets.

scenes.heading: Assembly plant report, March
scenes.say: The assembly plant's March report shows labor over budget and supplies under budget. It also shows a head-office IT allocation over budget, which the plant manager can't influence. Reports should separate it.

sub: Hold the manager with the best information
scenes.say: A better question than 'who controls it?' is 'who knows the most about it?' The purchasing manager can't set battery prices, but she should explain them and look for alternatives.
Performance reports work best as information for learning. Used only to blame, they encourage padding budgets and hiding problems.

scenes.q: Which item is least controllable by the assembly plant manager?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which item is least controllable by the assembly manager? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. Head-office IT costs are set elsewhere and allocated in.

videos.title: The sales-volume variance
videos.take: Sales-volume variance = (actual units − budgeted units) × budgeted contribution margin per unit

scenes.say: Tallgrass sold fewer bikes than planned. How much did that cost? The sales-volume variance answers that.

scenes.heading: 2027 budget and actual
scenes.say: The budget was nine hundred Trail bikes, with a contribution margin of $900 each, and three hundred Cargo bikes at $1,500. Actual sales were eight hundred eighty Trail bikes and two hundred twenty Cargo bikes.
The sales-volume variance is actual units minus budgeted units, times the budgeted contribution margin per unit. Using budgeted margins isolates the effect of volume alone.

scenes.heading: Sales-volume variance
scenes.say: Trail bikes: twenty short, times $900, $18,000 unfavorable. Cargo bikes: eighty short, times $1,500, $120,000 unfavorable. In total, selling fewer bikes cost $138,000 of contribution margin.
Recall from ACCT four thirteen: the static budget variance splits into a flexible-budget variance, about prices and costs, and this sales-volume variance. Now we dig into the volume part.

scenes.q: Budget 500 units, actual 540, budgeted CM $80. Sales-volume variance?
scenes.say: Quick check. Budget five hundred units, actual five forty, budgeted contribution margin eighty dollars. What's the sales-volume variance? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Forty extra units times $80 is $3,200 favorable.

videos.title: Sales-mix and sales-quantity variances
videos.take: The sales-volume variance splits into a mix effect and a quantity effect

scenes.say: Tallgrass sold fewer bikes overall, and a less profitable mix. Two variances separate those effects.

scenes.heading: Budgeted and actual mix
scenes.say: The budgeted mix was seventy-five percent Trail and twenty-five percent Cargo. The actual mix was eighty and twenty. At the budgeted mix, the average contribution margin per bike is $1,050.

scenes.heading: Sales-mix variance
scenes.say: The sales-mix variance takes total actual units times the change in mix times budgeted margin. Selling more Trail bikes adds $49,500. Selling fewer Cargo bikes costs $82,500. The shift toward the cheaper bike cost $33,000.

scenes.heading: Sales-quantity variance
scenes.say: The sales-quantity variance is the change in total units times the budgeted average margin: a hundred fewer bikes times $1,050, $105,000 unfavorable. Mix plus quantity gives the $138,000 sales-volume variance.
These point to different problems: the mix variance says customers chose the cheaper bike; the quantity variance says fewer bikes were sold overall.

scenes.q: Actual units equal budgeted units, but the mix shifted toward the high-CM product. Which variance is favorable?
scenes.say: Quick check. Total units hit budget, but the mix shifted toward the high-margin product. Which variance is favorable? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, sales mix. The quantity variance is zero.

videos.title: Market-share and market-size variances
videos.take: The sales-quantity variance splits into market-share and market-size effects

scenes.say: Did Tallgrass sell fewer bikes because the market shrank, or because competitors took share? Two more variances tell us.

scenes.heading: Upper Midwest e-bike market
scenes.say: Ana budgeted a regional market of twenty-four thousand e-bikes with a five percent share. The market actually grew to twenty-five thousand, but Tallgrass's share fell to four point four percent.

scenes.heading: Splitting the sales-quantity variance
scenes.say: The market-share variance is actual market size times the change in share, times budgeted average margin: $157,500 unfavorable. The market-size variance is the change in market size times budgeted share and margin: $52,500 favorable. Together, the $105,000.
This changes the story. Sales didn't fall because of a weak market; the market grew. Tallgrass lost share to competitors, which is a problem for marketing and product strategy.
These variances are only as good as the market-size data, which comes from industry associations, registrations or surveys.

scenes.q: Market fell from 10,000 to 9,000 units; budgeted share 10%; budgeted CM $200. Market-size variance?
scenes.say: Quick check. The market fell from ten thousand to nine thousand units, budgeted share ten percent, budgeted margin two hundred dollars. What's the market-size variance? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. A thousand fewer units times ten percent times $200: $20,000 unfavorable.

videos.title: Using sales variances
videos.take: Layered variances point to causes, but managers must still investigate

scenes.say: We've broken one disappointing number into four. Now, what should Ana tell the CEO?

scenes.heading: The variance tree
scenes.say: The sales-volume variance of $138,000 splits into a mix effect of $33,000 and a quantity effect of $105,000. Quantity splits into a share loss of $157,500, partly offset by $52,500 from a growing market.

scenes.heading: Questions to ask
items: Why did Cargo bikes lose share: price, range, competition?
Did dealers push the Trail bike over the Cargo?
Did a competitor launch a new model?
scenes.say: The variances point to questions. Why did the Cargo bike underperform? Did dealers push the cheaper Trail bike? Did a competitor launch something new? The numbers don't answer these; people do.
Responsibility follows. The marketing and sales teams answer for share and mix. No one at Tallgrass controls the size of the market.
Then act: perhaps dealer incentives for Cargo bikes, a review of competitors' models, or a product update. And next year's budget should use better market forecasts.

scenes.q: Which variance is least controllable by Tallgrass's marketing team?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which variance is least controllable by marketing? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. The size of the regional market depends on the economy and consumer trends.

warmup: A coffee shop sells fewer lattes than planned in a month when a new café opens next door, but the town has more tourists than usual. How would you separate the effects?
Market-size (more tourists) versus market-share (lost to the new café). Previews 5.5.
acts: Classify as cost, revenue, profit or investment center: (a) Tallgrass's paint shop, (b) e-commerce site that sets prices, (c) the whole company, (d) regional sales office paid on revenue.
Redesign the assembly plant report to separate controllable and uncontrollable items. Who should explain the IT allocation?
Show controllable items first; list allocations separately; head-office IT manager explains it.
Budget: A 600 units, CM $50; B 400, CM $80. Actual: A 650, B 300. Compute sales-volume variances.
Same data: budgeted mix 60/40; actual 950 units (68.4%/31.6%). Budgeted average CM $62. Compute mix and quantity variances.
Budget market 20,000 units, share 5%; actual market 19,000, share 5%. Budgeted average CM $62. Market-share and market-size variances?
Draft a one-paragraph memo to Tallgrass's CEO summarizing the 2027 sales variances.
Volume $138,000 U: mostly lost share ($157,500 U) in a growing market ($52,500 F) and a shift away from Cargo bikes ($33,000 U). Recommend reviewing Cargo competitiveness and dealer incentives.
case: Tallgrass's 2027 results show the variances in this lecture. Dealers report that a competitor launched a cargo e-bike with longer range at $3,300, and that Tallgrass pays dealers the same 8% commission on both models. The sales director is paid a bonus on total units sold.
Which variances does this information help explain?
How might the bonus and commission structure affect mix?

It explains the share and mix variances. Equal commissions and a units-based bonus encourage selling easier, cheaper Trail bikes; reward contribution margin instead (or higher commission on Cargo). Consider a range upgrade or price response on the Cargo. Monitor share, mix and margin, not just units.
exam: Explain the four types of responsibility center and give an example of each.
Cost (assembly plant), revenue (sales team), profit (online store/parts business), investment (division or company).
Budget: X 800 units CM $40, Y 200 units CM $90 (mix 80/20). Actual: X 900, Y 150. Compute the sales-volume, sales-mix and sales-quantity variances.

Volume: X 4,000 F; Y 4,500 U; total 500 U. Budgeted average CM 50. Actual 1,050 units (85.7/14.3). Mix: X 1,050 × 5.71% × 40 = 2,400 F; Y 1,050 × −5.71% × 90 = 5,400 U; mix 3,000 U. Quantity: 50 × 50 = 2,500 F. Total 500 U.

ex.q: Match each unit to its type of responsibility center.
ex.why: Each center is accountable for what it controls.

ex.q: Which question best guides who should explain a variance?
opts: Who has the most information about it?
ex.why: Responsibility accounting holds the best-informed manager accountable for explaining an item.

ex.q: Budget 700 units, actual 650, budgeted CM $120. Sales-volume variance (enter as a negative number if unfavorable)?
Total actual units 2,000; a product's mix rose from 30% to 35%; its budgeted CM is $40. Its sales-mix variance?
Budgeted total units 1,000; actual 1,080; budgeted average CM $60. Sales-quantity variance?
Actual market 50,000; actual share 9%, budgeted share 10%; budgeted average CM $30. Market-share variance (negative if unfavorable)?
Order the variances from broadest to narrowest.
ex.why: Volume splits into mix and quantity; quantity into share and size.

ex.q: The market grew but Tallgrass's units fell. Which variance must be unfavorable?
ex.why: A growing market gives a favorable size variance, so falling units mean share was lost.
